analysis:
Integration of the fast-reconnect change. The PR adds CoordinatorReconnectPolicy (60 s stable-session backoff reset; close code 1012 gives a random 0-1 s wait without growing the backoff). The changes consist of a CoordinatorSessionRecorder in CoordinatorClientState.swift, a reconnectPolicy init parameter in CoordinatorClient.swift, a close-code capture in CoordinatorClient+Connection.swift (including sentCloseCode, which reads the first two payload bytes when Network.framework reports noStatusReceived), tests, MockCoordinator.dropActiveWebSocket(closeCode:reason:), and docs. Checked against TB-002, TB-011, T-053, T-010 and A-018. Replayed head evidence shows the design is consistent with the threat model.

Observed controls: the recorder holds a non-secret integer code and open time under a lock. The documented sentCloseCode parse checks content.count >= 2. Only the close code is used, not the reason. The receive loop still throws on a .close opcode before JSON handling. Every reconnect sends a fresh register, so attestation, the per-socket nonce and connection-bound authorization (T-053, TB-011) are unchanged. The close code comes from the trusted coordinator over TLS, so the worst case is shorter reconnect timing, an availability matter only. No encryption, key, cache (T-041) or hold-socket (TB-012) behavior changes. Test and mock changes are test-only, loopback-bound and not shipped.

Residual unverified contracts: the production CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift and CoordinatorSessionEnd were not supplied as full source. I could not confirm that delay ranges are bounded and non-negative, that a rapid repeated 1012 loop is limited (the 0 s lower bound permits an immediate retry and the backoff never grows on 1012), that Double.random on a degenerate range is safe, or that the recorder is created per attempt. These are availability and reconnect-storm concerns, not demonstrated regressions. No finding is raised. A code-level check of the policy file is recommended.
